placeholders.C: correction prefix solved by the probe (e.g. '../../'), inserted immediately before P
placeholders.FWAT: fullwidth commercial at, U+FF20 (unicode look-alike of @)
placeholders.AFW: allowed host with every ASCII char mapped to its Unicode fullwidth form (e.g. 'e' -> 'ｅ')
placeholders.TFW: target host with every ASCII char mapped to its Unicode fullwidth form
placeholders.FWBS: fullwidth reverse solidus, U+FF3C (unicode look-alike of backslash)

techniques.name: Simple userinfo @
techniques.description: The allowed host appears in plain sight before an @; the real host (userinfo delimiter) is whatever follows it. Fools naive startsWith/contains checks while the real client connects to the target.

techniques.name: Double @ (target-allowed-target)
techniques.description: Two @ signs: target, then allowed, then target again. Useful to probe whether a parser treats the first or the last @ as the userinfo/host separator.

techniques.name: Double @ (allowed-allowed-target)
techniques.description: The allowed domain appears twice before a final @ followed by the target. A naive 'startsWith(allowed@)' check passes, while a last-@ parser lands on the target.

techniques.name: Invalid port userinfo decoy
techniques.description: The allowed domain followed by ':' and the target, as if the target were an invalid port, before the real @ that terminates the userinfo.

techniques.name: Backslash before @
techniques.description: A backslash inserted before the @. WHATWG-family parsers normalize \ to / in 'special' schemes, which can shift the authority boundary.

techniques.name: Double backslash
techniques.description: Two backslashes between allowed and target, no @. Tests whether the parser treats them as authority/path separators.

techniques.name: Single backslash
techniques.description: A single backslash between allowed and target.

techniques.name: Backslash then double @
techniques.description: Backslash followed by two consecutive @ signs (empty userinfo in between). Breaks differently depending on whether the parser treats the backslash as an authority terminator or as a literal character before looking for @.

techniques.name: Scheme with a single slash
techniques.description: '{S}:/' instead of '{S}://' before the authority. Some lenient parsers still recognize an authority.

techniques.name: Triple slash before authority
techniques.description: An extra slash right after '{S}://' before the userinfo/host.

techniques.name: Direct target, allowed hidden in fragment
techniques.description: The real host is already the target; the allowed domain only appears in the fragment (#) to fool a naive 'contains(allowed)' check that never does real parsing.

techniques.name: Direct target, allowed hidden in query
techniques.description: Same idea as fragment-hides-target but via a query string ('?').

techniques.name: Tab before @
techniques.description: A tab character (U+0009) inserted before the @. Many parsers silently strip tabs/CR/LF anywhere in the URL (WHATWG), which can break a naive check while leaving the real parse intact.

techniques.name: Carriage return before @
techniques.description: A raw CR (U+000D) inserted before the @. Some parsers strip it globally before parsing (reaching the target cleanly), others treat it as an invalid/terminating character within the authority.

techniques.name: Line feed before @
techniques.description: A raw LF (U+000A) inserted before the @, same idea as the CR variant.

techniques.name: CRLF before @
techniques.description: A raw CRLF pair inserted before the @.

techniques.name: Vertical tab before @
techniques.description: A vertical tab (U+000B) inserted before the @ - less commonly special-cased than TAB/CR/LF, so parser coverage of it is more likely to diverge.

techniques.name: Form feed before @
techniques.description: A form feed (U+000C) inserted before the @.

techniques.name: Percent-encoded NUL before @
techniques.description: A percent-encoded NUL byte (%00) inserted before the @. Tests whether a parser decodes it before authority splitting (unusual) versus keeps it as a literal, inert three-character sequence.

techniques.name: Leading empty userinfo
techniques.description: A bare @ right after the scheme (empty userinfo) before the allowed host, then a second @ before the target. Tests whether a parser's 'last @ wins' rule is truly global or gets confused by the empty first segment.

techniques.name: Userinfo with empty password
techniques.description: Allowed host followed by a bare trailing colon (empty password) before the real @.

techniques.name: Percent-encoded @ only (no raw @)
techniques.description: Uses %40 instead of a raw @ between allowed and target, with no real @ anywhere. Tests whether a parser pre-decodes percent-escapes before splitting the authority (rare, but ground truth beats assumption here).

techniques.name: Allowed host wrapped in brackets
techniques.description: The allowed host wrapped in [] (normally reserved for IPv6 literals) right before the @. Tests how a parser that expects only an IPv6 address inside brackets reacts to an arbitrary string there.

techniques.name: Target host wrapped in brackets
techniques.description: The target host wrapped in [] right after the @.

techniques.name: Backslashes right after scheme
techniques.description: Both scheme slashes replaced by backslashes (scheme colon followed directly by two backslashes) instead of the normal two forward slashes.

techniques.name: Mixed slash/backslash after scheme
techniques.description: One forward slash then one backslash before the authority, instead of two forward slashes.

techniques.name: Fullwidth unicode @ (U+FF20)
techniques.description: Uses the fullwidth commercial-at look-alike (U+FF20) instead of a real @, with no ASCII @ anywhere. Tests whether a parser's hostname/IDNA normalization maps it back to a real delimiter.

techniques.name: Control char 0x01 before @
techniques.description: Raw byte 0x01 inserted before the @, as part of a systematic sweep of the full C0 control range plus space/DEL — some parsers strip/reject specific control bytes while others pass them through as literal authority characters.

techniques.name: Zero scheme slashes + userinfo @
techniques.description: Scheme colon directly followed by the authority (no slashes at all), combined with the userinfo @ trick. Inspired by the cheat sheet's bare 'http:ATTACKERHOSTNAME' / 'http:@ATTACKERHOSTNAME' entries.

techniques.name: Backslash-slash in path (protocol-relative via backslash)
techniques.description: A path starting with backslash-then-slash: WHATWG normalizes the backslash to a slash, turning '/\\target' into '//target' - a scheme-relative authority reinterpretation. Inspired by the cheat sheet's bare path-trick entries ('/\\ATTACKERHOSTNAME').

techniques.name: Backslash-slash-backslash-slash path
techniques.description: Alternating backslash/slash pairs before the target. Inspired by the cheat sheet's '\\/\\/ATTACKERHOSTNAME' entry.

techniques.name: Backslash-slash path (single pair)
techniques.description: Inspired by the cheat sheet's '\\/ATTACKERHOSTNAME' entry.

techniques.name: Bracketed allowed sandwich before target
techniques.description: Allowed host wrapped in [] (IPv6-literal syntax) twice before the real @-delimited target. Inspired by the cheat sheet's '[::1]@[::1]@ATTACKERHOSTNAME' entry.

techniques.name: Fullwidth-encoded target host
techniques.description: The target host is spelled entirely with Unicode fullwidth characters (e.g. 'evil.example' -> 'ｅｖｉｌ．ｅｘａｍｐｌｅ'). Several parsers apply Unicode/IDNA host mapping that silently folds fullwidth forms back to plain ASCII, so they still connect to the target - while looking nothing like it to a naive string check.

techniques.name: Fullwidth target host, allowed hidden in fragment
techniques.description: Combines the fullwidth-host trick with hiding the allowed host in the fragment: the real host is the fullwidth-spelled target (normalized back to ASCII by IDNA-aware parsers), and the allowed domain only appears after '#' to fool a naive contains() check.

techniques.name: IPv6 zone-ID as userinfo decoy
techniques.description: The allowed host is smuggled inside an IPv6 zone identifier (the '%25' + text after an IPv6 literal, e.g. link-local scope id) used as userinfo, before the real @-delimited target. Tests whether a parser's IPv6-literal-with-zone-id grammar is lenient enough to just skip over the whole bracketed mess.

techniques.name: Real @ then backslash-@ (allowed first)
techniques.description: Allowed host, a real @, then a backslash immediately followed by another @, then target. Refines the plain backslash-@ trick: works only for parsers that don't lock in the first real @ as decisive even when a later backslash+@ sequence follows.

techniques.name: Non-breaking space before @
techniques.description: A non-breaking space (U+00A0) inserted before the @. Outside the ASCII C0 control range already swept elsewhere - tests a different 'is this whitespace' code path than tab/CR/LF.

techniques.name: Zero-width space before @
techniques.description: A zero-width space (U+200B, a formatting character with no visual width) inserted before the @ - invisible when the payload is displayed or logged.

techniques.name: Tab between scheme and colon, allowed in fragment
techniques.description: A tab character between the scheme name and its colon (e.g. 'http\t://'), combined with hiding the allowed host in the fragment. Tests whitespace tolerance at the scheme/colon boundary specifically, not just inside the authority.

techniques.name: Space between scheme and colon, allowed in fragment
techniques.description: Same idea as scheme-colon-tab but with a plain space.

techniques.name: Semicolon before @
techniques.description: A semicolon inserted right before the @ - an old RFC 2396 path/userinfo parameter delimiter that no longer means anything special in modern URL grammars. Reaches the target on every parser tested, since it's simply extra literal userinfo content before a normal @, but it reliably breaks naive contains()/startsWith() checks that don't expect a ';' there.

techniques.name: Fullwidth backslash before @
techniques.description: The fullwidth reverse solidus look-alike (U+FF3C) used instead of a real backslash, right before the @. Extends the backslash family into Unicode look-alike territory.
